title: Upper Lower 2 days Program review
summary: NH reviews a subscriber's upper/lower program (two days run twice a week), which is cable- and machine-heavy and has no squats or deadlifts because of an ab weakness. He recommends starting with compound strength work, supersetting antagonists and using giant sets, adding volume for pulls, hamstrings and calves, and matching rep ranges to how prone each movement is to mechanical failure.

claims.claim: Before reviewing a program, read the lifter's goals and limitations.
Leanness depends on both cardio and calories, and you can lose fat without being in a deficit.
The neck is an important muscle to train; he gained half an inch on his and likes the look, but it's optional if yours is already in proportion.
Two repeating days means low exercise selection, which limits progress somewhat, though there's no need for more days if you're progressing.
Frequency, volume within a session and sets/reps per session all matter for growth; short programs either under-train some muscles or stimulate none of them enough for impressive growth.
Novices need less volume and intermediates more; some people respond to intensity while others get sick on high volume.
He doesn't like starting a session with cable work; begin with strength work such as dumbbell bench (an admitted bias).
Supersetting dumbbell bench (4x10-15) with cable rows trains antagonists, is healthy for the shoulders and boosts conditioning and metabolism; match the rows to 4 sets.
Do more pulling than pushing, because the upper back has more potential for strength and size.
One-arm dumbbell rows after cable rows are fine because the unilateral, against-gravity pull works a different plane.
Follow chest and back strength work with lighter isolation for squeeze and focus on the muscle.
12-20 reps is a very good range for shrugs.
Isolation work at the end can stay at 3 higher-rep sets and be pushed hard because those movements aren't dangerous.
Triceps extensions, face pulls and cable curls work different muscles and can form a giant set, but don't put two biceps movements back to back.

He has never met anyone who built an impressive natural physique mainly with cables, and sees a correlation between heavy cable users and people who don't get big; he uses cables as finishing work for angles and tension.
If you can, do a heavy knee-flexion movement and a heavy hip hinge from the floor (any variation); you need them to grow.

Cable movements tend to cause mechanical failure before muscular failure; on cables you can keep moving with body English while the muscle stops being recruited, whereas with free weights the set simply ends.
Leg extensions can be dangerous for some people because loading the top of the knee in extension stresses the joint.
Hamstrings are a bigger muscle group and need more work: at least 4x15 curls, supersetted with leg extensions.
Start the lower day with the leg press as strength work, not with isolation; don't waste your energy on isolation first.
Wide rep ranges (12-20) suit movements prone to mechanical failure like cable rows; for the leg press, which can only be cheated by shortening ROM, use 4x12-15 to stay accountable.
People who plan to train abs or calves at home rarely do; train them at the gym.
Supersetting single-leg calf raises with the leg press won't fatigue you and can improve mind-muscle connection; do 4x25, plus weighted calf stretches at 4x10.
On a low-volume upper body day, fixed rep ranges are fine: keep the volume steady and push the weight; it only becomes a problem if progress stops.
Use a fixed 3x12 for lateral raises because mechanical failure comes easily, unless you have very good delt control.
Evolving ranges are fine for rope pushdowns because failure there is usually true triceps failure, unless you start swinging.
Don't superset dips with shoulder press, since both hit the lateral and medial triceps heads; laterals and pushdowns can be supersetted.
